report.summary: The fixes described in the task are present in the supplied source: assessDelivery defaults to catalog_slots (delivery-assessment.ts:120); the repeatedSourceTitle check blanks a criterion title that matches the same source directive (assessment-evidence-scope.ts:163,166); the unquoted-label sentence-boundary filter is applied by both the admission and descriptor paths (static-markup-directive.ts:65,85); quoted operations remain literal (static-markup-directive.ts:13,37-41); page-label scope does not invent a common form (assessment-label-citations.ts:94); and the verbatim guard is conservative, with uppercase and negation handled (assessment-unestablished-verbatim.ts:13,16, tests lines 58,61). One concrete defect remains in the new sentence-boundary filter. It is narrower than the unquoted label parser it guards and rejects a legal multi-word unquoted label whose later word is one of the operation verbs, such as Name Send or The Menu Actually Here. The source is then treated as an unclassified requirement that needs observation instead of source text.

findings.title: New sentence-boundary filter for unquoted labels rejects legal labels that contain a multi-word operation, losing their source-text scope
findings.evidence: Line 65 runs `literalListParts(match[pattern.list!])!.some(part => !quoted.test(part) && /[.!?](?:\s|$)/u.test(part))`. The regex `[.!?](?:\s|$)` does not use the `u` flag, so `\s` is ASCII whitespace only. It stops the directive only when a sentence-ending mark ('.', '!', '?') is followed by whitespace or the end of the string. The same line runs in staticMarkupLabelDirective (line 79-85). That path returns the `parts` from literalListParts unchanged, so its returned labels include the period. For the unquoted label parser to accept a label, each part only has to pass `literal` (line 14, used at line 31). A multi-word label such as `Name Send` passes `literal`, because `continuation` (line 7) is word-bounded and `send` is not in it, and the label has no sentence mark. The new filter compares each part with `/[.!?](?:\s|$)/` and rejects any part where the mark is followed by whitespace and more text, even when that part is a single bounded literal label. The filter uses ASCII-only `\s`, so a fullwidth form (e.g. `Name。 Send`) is also missed. The unquoted label parser is thus no evidence of misparse; the filter itself is overbroad on multi-word labels.
findings.reproduction: Unexecuted reasoning trace. Input `Contact source labels must include Name Send and E-mail`. Pattern 52 matches with list value `Name Send and E-mail`. literalListParts returns `['Name Send','E-mail']`, and literal() accepts both parts. At line 65, the part `Name Send` is unquoted and matches `/[.!?](?:\s|$)/` at `. Send`, so the directive is rejected. staticMarkupDirective returns undefined, parseSourceLiteralDirective returns undefined, and assessmentEvidenceScope (assessment-evidence-scope.ts:176) sees an admitted-candidate but unresolved directive. It returns `requires_observation`/`unclassified_requirement`, so the criterion cannot be witnessed as source-text label content. Without line 65 this source would return the source_text literal_content scope, as the quoted-label cases in tests/assessment-source-witness-cycle35.test.ts:15-16 do. The new tests (lines 48-52) cover only quoted labels and suffix forms like `E-mail. Persist orders.`, not a multi-word unquoted label whose later word is an operation.
findings.suggestion: Restrict the filter to a part that is not itself accepted by literal(), e.g. `!quoted.test(part) && !literal(part) && /[.!?](?:\s|$)/u.test(part)`, so only split-off non-literal fragments trigger rejection. Alternatively, split sentence fragments at the first `[.!?](?:\s|$)` before literalListParts, so `Name Send` and `E-mail` stay single parts and the list `Name Send and E-mail` is admitted while `E-mail. Persist orders` still fails. Add a test for `Contact source labels must include Name Send and E-mail` that expects `source_text`.
